items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: Retro Techno Generator: Your Pulse Plays 90s Acid Techno, Your Dancing Plays the Filters
items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge This article provides a step by step guide to Retro Techno Generator, a music toy built on the Presage SmartSpectra SDK for Node.js. A webcam reads your pulse, breathing and facial expressions, and a browser page turns them into 90s acid techno and hardcore with Web Audio. Every sound is synthesised; there are no samples. https://github.com/xbill9/retro-techno-generator Your breathing and pulse steer the music, your face plays the lead, and your dancing opens the filters. Pulse and breathing need you to hold still, and the music asks you to move, so the app makes the two take turns: dance and the movement drives the sound, freeze for a few seconds and it re-reads your pulse. A hard dance raises your pulse, and the next still moment pushes the tempo up. A Node server runs a SmartSpectra session on the local camera and streams the signals over a WebSocket to a page on localhost. The page is the instrument: a 16-step sequencer, a 303-style acid line, drum synthesis, pads, piano stabs and a hoover, all built from Web Audio oscillators and filters. Signal What it plays Pulse Tempo is pulse × 2, held between 100 and 190 BPM.

items.title: How I Built a YouTube Music App UI Using React Native and Expo
items.summary: Building a music streaming application is a great way to explore mobile app development beyond basic screens and navigation. Recently, I worked on a YouTube Music-inspired mobile application using React Native and Expo. The goal was to create a modern music application experience with music discovery, playlists, an interactive music player, and actual audio playback functionality. In this article, I'll walk through the project, its main features, the technologies used, and some of the development concepts involved. If you're learning React Native or looking for practical mobile app development projects, this walkthrough may be useful. The project is a music player application inspired by the familiar experience of YouTube Music. items.title: Hangfire Alternative in .NET: Why I Replaced It With BackgroundService and Channel
items.summary: The first version of this site was an ASP.NET Core MVC app with Hangfire wired in: a dashboard at /hangfire, five recurring jobs, ten places in the code that called BackgroundJob.Enqueue, and a second SQL Server database just to hold Hangfire's job tables. When I rewrote the backend as a separate Web API, I didn't bring Hangfire with me. The API that serves this page runs two BackgroundService classes fed by System.Threading.Channels, and one WHERE clause does the work of the every-minute job. This isn't a "Hangfire is bad" post. Hangfire is a good library. It's a post about checking which jobs actually needed it, because for this site the answer was none of them. The short version: Use Hangfire (or Quartz.NET) when a job must survive a restart, retry on its own, or be visible on a dashboard. If the work is in-process, short-lived and fine to lose on a crash, a BackgroundService with a bounded Channel is built into .NET, needs no extra database, and is about 60 lines. When people need to hide an Aadhaar number, PAN, SSN, or bank account balance on a PDF, they often open a free online PDF editor, draw a black rectangle over the text, and hit save. items.title: Subresource Integrity (SRI): Pin Your CDN Scripts
items.summary: Every on your site is a standing grant of full JavaScript execution to whoever controls that file tomorrow. Not the file you reviewed, the file the CDN serves on the next request. Subresource Integrity (SRI) is the one browser feature that turns that open grant into a fixed contract: run this exact file, byte for byte, or run nothing. I run PixelValut, a set of browser-side developer and security tools, and SRI is one of the cheapest controls I know with real teeth. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command and claim myself. All outputs below are from commands I ran today in a terminal and in Chrome 156 driven by Playwright. Direct answer: SRI makes the browser hash a downloaded script or stylesheet and compare it with the integrity value in your HTML. If one byte differs, the browser blocks the file. It protects against a compromised CDN or a hijacked file. It needs crossorigin="anonymous" and a CORS-enabled host, and it only works for static, versioned files. items.summary: The U.S. Treasury publishes savings bond values through its Savings Bonds Value Files dataset. Its sb_value endpoint returns an issue year in each row, with separate amount fields for January through December. That shape creates two easy data-import mistakes: treating a missing cell as zero, and converting decimal dollar strings through floating-point arithmetic before exporting cents. Here is a small Node.js workflow that keeps those cases separate and produces a CSV suitable for a spreadsheet or a historical-data pipeline. items.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
items.summary: Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development. The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: I run Stockinsky, a small site that writes paid AI research reports on listed companies. Most companies will never get a paid report, but people still search for them by name. So I added a free page for every stock: ten years of financials, a red-flag checklist, dividend history and the latest close. There are now about 2,000 China A-share pages, plus around 530 Hong Kong and 530 U.S. ones. Here is how they are built, and the one incident that shaped the design. The first version fetched data when someone opened a page and cached the result. That works fine for people. It does not work for crawlers. A search engine bot can open hundreds of stock pages in a few minutes, and every cache miss turns into several requests to free market-data endpoints. Then I made it worse myself. I ran a bulk measurement script on the production server, and the quote provider started rate-limiting the server's IP. Live quotes on the site broke for real users. The site and my batch job shared one IP, so the batch job took the site down with it. After that I set one rule: the server only reads files. All fetching happens on my own machine. items.title: When “Working as Designed” Is the Problem
items.summary: I submitted a security report to Anthropic after Claude Code exposed my .NET User Secrets in its model context. They classified it as “Informative – Working as Designed.” “Working as designed” is a triage label, not a verdict. But taken at face value, it points to something architectural: security is enforced tool by tool, not around the agent as a whole, and certainly not at the OS-boundary level. .NET developers commonly use dotnet user-secrets to keep development credentials in their user profile, outside the project tree. These secrets can include: • API keys • Database connection strings • Passwords • Third-party service credentials • Other sensitive application configuration Consider this scenario: You have a .NET application. You have configured User Secrets. You launch Claude Code in your project directory. You ask Claude to inspect your application configuration. Claude can execute: dotnet user-secrets list And/or read the plaintext secrets.json file. %APPDATA%\Microsoft\UserSecrets\ \secrets.json Because tool output is returned to Claude, those credentials become part of the conversation context. items.title: Keep AI-suggested loading skeletons matched to real content height
items.summary: Agents love inventing skeleton screens. Ask for a loading state and you get a neat gray card with three lines… that is half the height of the real content. When data arrives, the layout jumps. CLS goes up. Reviewers shrug because “at least there is a skeleton.” I’ve started treating height match as a hard constraint, not a nice-to-have. If the skeleton doesn’t reserve roughly the same vertical space as the loaded UI, send it back. AI drafts tend to: Copy a generic “3 lines + avatar” pattern from training data Ignore the real card’s padding, media block, or multi-row meta Use fixed h-4 bars that look pretty in isolation and wrong in the page Forget mobile denser layouts vs desktop taller cards The PR still “has a loading state,” so it merges. items.title: Your chart library doesn't need a dark mode
items.summary: A Recharts chart can follow your page's dark mode with no theme state and no re-render: it names CSS variables, and the page declares them. This article shows the container that declares them, the trap that catches the hand-written version, and what still needs a line of your own. The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article. A chart library takes its colours as strings — stroke="#0ea5e9" — so nothing your page does to its own theme reaches the chart. Your cards turn dark and the chart keeps its light-mode lines, black axis labels and a white tooltip. The fixes land one bug at a time: axis labels in one project, tooltips in another, labels, series and tooltips in a third, all in the last three months. Recharts itself discussed a theming API through most of 2026 and is shipping one in its 3.11 pre-releases, marked experimental. The usual fixes each cost something: Pick the colour in React: stroke={theme === 'dark' ? '#38bdf8' : '#0ea5e9'}. Every chart reads the theme, so every chart re-renders on a switch, and a server render has to guess the theme. Variables in a global stylesheet. items.title: Next.js 15 is a one-line upgrade. The breaking changes are in every file that reads a cookie.
items.summary: Upgrading to Next.js 15 is one line: - "next": "14.2.15" + "next": "15.0.3" The work is in the files that line affects. Three changes cause most of it. cookies(), headers() and draftMode() now return promises. import { cookies } from "next/headers"; export default async function Page() { - const theme = cookies().get("theme"); + const theme = (await cookies()).get("theme"); ... } Next.js keeps a temporary synchronous fallback that logs a warning, which is kind for the upgrade and unkind for finding the problem: the code keeps working, and the warning sits in your logs. In route params, the same applies: params and searchParams in pages and layouts are promises too. fetch() isn't cached by default In 14, fetch() in a server component was cached unless you opted out. In 15 it isn't cached unless you opt in: await fetch(url, { cache: "force-cache" }); Nothing breaks. Some pages that were fast because of a cache you never meant to rely on get slower. Same idea for app/**/route.ts: a GET handler is dynamic by default now. Add export const dynamic = "force-static" where you really wanted it cached. While capital cities often attract telemedicine startups and digital health investments, regional districts and tier-2 cities are frequently left navigating fragmented, pen-and-paper systems. Patients in district headquarters like Feni Sadar (Bangladesh) regularly struggle with: Finding verified, BMDC-registered specialist doctors and their updated chamber visiting hours. Unpredictable, out-of-pocket diagnostic lab expenses. Lack of transparent emergency ambulance contacts during critical golden hours. To bridge this gap, we engineered and launched Health Club Feni—a modern, full-stack digital healthcare directory and membership network designed specifically for the local ecosystem. (Note: Despite the name, Health Club is strictly a medical care directory and membership platform, not an athletic fitness gym). items.title: React: un presupuesto de foco para interfaces rápidas
items.summary: La accesibilidad y el rendimiento suelen revisarse en tickets distintos. En una interfaz real, sin embargo, el usuario los vive juntos: pulsa un botón, aparece un estado de carga, el foco cambia (o se pierde) y la pantalla vuelve a pintar. Si esa secuencia no está diseñada, una mejora visual puede sentirse como un fallo. Este patrón es especialmente útil en formularios de registro, verificación y pruebas de email. Incluso cuando alguien busca tempmailso para validar un flujo, la experiencia no debería depender de adivinar donde quedó el cursor. Llamo “presupuesto de foco” a una regla simple: cada interacción debe mover el foco solo cuando existe una razón clara. Por ejemplo: Si el usuario abre un diálogo, el foco entra al diálogo y vuelve al control que lo abrió al cerrarlo. Si un formulario falla, el foco puede ir al primer error solo después de que el usuario intentó enviarlo. Si una operación tarda, el foco permanece donde estaba mientras el estado de carga se anuncia. El error común es enfocar siempre el primer elemento que cambia. items.title: Permission-heavy multi-tenant systems: make the access check boring
items.summary: Permission-heavy systems become risky when access rules are scattered across controllers, UI checks, repository filters, and background jobs. The aim is not a clever authorization framework. It is one rule path that is difficult to bypass. The examples come from Shield, Zotic, CAS, Question Banking and Amlaak. Every protected operation can be described with four values: the actor, the tenant, the action, and the resource. If one is unknown, the system does not yet have enough information to allow the operation. This simple tuple prevents a common mistake: checking that a user has a permission somewhere, then loading a resource that belongs to another tenant. Permission and ownership need to be evaluated together. The decision input public sealed record AccessRequest( Guid ActorId, Guid TenantId, string Action, string ResourceType, Guid? ResourceId); A route parameter or request body can name a tenant, but it cannot prove membership in that tenant. Resolve the active tenant from authenticated membership, then compare any requested tenant identifier with it. items.title: Building a service status notifier with .NET and Cloudflare Workers
items.summary: I've been working on a small side project recently. Like most developers I depend on quite a few external services. GitHub, Cloudflare, OpenAI, and others. When something breaks, I usually end up checking their individual status pages to figure out what's going on. I wanted a simpler way to keep track of these incidents and get notified in Slack without having to configure every provider separately. So I started building StatusRelay. Why build another status monitoring tool? Of course, tools like this already exist, and they offer much more comprehensive solutions. I wasn't trying to reinvent everything they do. I just wanted something lightweight where I could select the services I care about, connect a Slack channel or webhook, and start receiving notifications. No accounts, no paid plans, and no complicated setup. It also seemed like a fun opportunity to experiment with event processing, background jobs, and reliable notification delivery. But how does it work?! The idea is pretty straightforward: Poll official status APIs from different providers. Normalize their status and incident information. Store incidents and detect changes. Send notifications to Slack or custom webhooks.

items.title: Building MCP Servers in .NET for AI Agents, a 10-part tutorial series
items.summary: If you're a .NET developer and you want to build an MCP server, it's hard to know where to start. Most examples stop at a "hello world" tool running on your own machine. I wanted a series that goes from that first tool all the way to a server that real users can sign in to and use from different AI clients. So I wrote one. It's 10 parts, it's free, and it's built on .NET 10 and ASP.NET Core from start to finish. The whole series builds one sample app, BitOfTech Expenses, an MCP server for expense reports and approvals. Each part adds to the one before it, so by the end you have a complete, working server and not a set of separate demos. By the end of the series, you'll have: A working MCP server in C# with tools, resources and prompts, connected to a real database and an external API. The server hosted in ASP.NET Core and secured with Microsoft Entra ID, so each user only sees and runs the tools they're allowed to use. A deployment on Azure Container Apps that you can use from VS Code Copilot, Claude, your own .NET agent and Microsoft Foundry. The company also announced Northstar, a new methalox booster engine that it says produces 715,000 pounds of thrust while cutting mass by 30% and parts by 50% compared with the BE-4. Space.com reports: The new stage will be powered by one BE-7 engine, which the company developed for use on its Blue Moon spacecraft, one of the two private vehicles that NASA selected to be crewed lunar landers for its Artemis program. items.title: Building a modern Blazor UI without leaving .NET: introducing RaxUI
items.summary: Why I built it I'm a full-stack developer. My backends are .NET, and for years my frontends were React and Next.js. I tried Blazor more than once, because I wanted one platform from the database to the browser. Each time a project needed a modern, highly customized interface, I ended up reaching for React and its component ecosystem again. So I started building the components I was missing, in Blazor, with the look and the developer experience I was used to. That work became RaxUI. RaxUI is a set of 68 open-source components for Blazor and React that share one theme. A CLI copies each component's source into your app, so you own the code and can change any of it. Your code, not a dependency. raxui add copies .razor files and their CSS into your project. Installed components run without the CLI, and there is no runtime package to upgrade. Modern components out of the box. Buttons and forms, but also a data grid, charts, a kanban board, a calendar, a command palette, chat and AI conversation parts, and a rich text editor. One theme, full control. Three appearances (default, flat, glass), light and dark mode, accent colours and density, all set with HTML attributes on any element. Rig

items.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
items.summary: I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock. So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted. DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all. The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero. I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
items.summary: "OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article: Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments: - Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled. - Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use.

items.title: OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
items.summary: A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports: Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes. items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Discord Is Ditching Electron For Rust
items.summary: Discord is replacing Electron with a desktop client built fully in Rust, which the company says should significantly reduce the app's notoriously high resource usage while improving performance and memory safety. "We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there," explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. "That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust." The Verge reports: Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app. It's not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company "hope to get it into testing with users soon." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.title: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. Coding agents in a native Mac app
items.summary: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. I built Coincide as a native Mac app for the coding agents I already use. Here is a new 10-second motion preview: A Mac interface built with Swift and AppKit Coincide's main interface is built with AppKit, with SwiftUI where it fits, such as Settings. It brings native menus, Mac keyboard shortcuts, a native transcript and the agent/model picker into one window. The clip calls out the architecture: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. That describes Coincide's Mac interface. It isn't a benchmark or a claim that every workload is faster than another app. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode and Antigravity each run through their own command-line tool and existing login. Coincide does not sell or meter tokens. When you switch agents mid-thread, the next agent gets a recap of the turns it missed and works in the same directory. Each agent keeps its own native session. Switching back resumes that agent's session. The handoff deep dive covers the mechanism and its limits. The preview browses Codex, Claude Code and Cursor's picker catalogs. items.title: Crop Once, Post Everywhere: Batch Aspect-Ratio Crops for Social Images in Swift
items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. Aspect-fit pad: show the whole photo, add bars (or a mat) to reach the ratio. For social uploads you almost always want (1). Padding changes the look of the feed thumbnail; a filled crop matches what creators already do in Instagram’s own editor. Centre-weighted aspect-fill is a good default. Face-awa

items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. You type to search, press ↵, and the item is pasted back into that app. Your eyes don't travel and your hands don't leave the keyboard. That needs three things macOS doesn't hand you directly: the caret's position in someone else's app, a sensible answer when that app won't tell you, a window that takes keystrokes without taking focus away from the app you're typing in. Here is how each one works, with code from the app, shortened. There's no "where is the caret" API on macOS. There is the Accessibility API, the one assistive apps like VoiceOver use to read other apps' interfaces. Your app needs the Accessibility permission for it (AXIsProcessTrusted() tells you whether you have it), and then it can ask three questions: Which element has keyboard focus? Ask the system-wide element for kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute. What's selected in it? kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute returns a CFRange. With nothing selected, it's an empty range at the caret. items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.
